section_summary: This section documents Japanese purchases and prospective purchases of scrap iron, graphite, ores, sulfur, zinc, copper, industrial machinery, fuel-processing technology, and other strategic materials from the Americas, Europe, and Asia. Consular and military reports repeatedly assess whether this trade reflected ordinary commercial expansion or preparations for war, while correspondence from private citizens urged restrictions on American scrap-metal exports. The papers also include statistical enclosures, internal routing memoranda, cross-reference sheets, duplicate despatch copies, and State Department replies explaining that existing law did not authorize restrictions on scrap exports.

subfiles.title: Opinion on authority to sell government vessels solely for scrapping
subfiles.from: Homer Cummings, Attorney General
subfiles.about: Concludes that existing merchant-marine legislation does not authorize the sale for scrap of vessels whose operating value substantially exceeds their scrap value.
subfiles.summary: Cummings rejects an earlier interpretation by Attorney General Sargent that broad sale conditions permitted the government to require scrapping. He advises that Congress should enact clarifying legislation if such a policy is desired.

subfiles.title: Increased Purchases by Japan of Ceylon Scrap Iron and Plumbago
subfiles.from: Robert L. Buell, American Consul at Colombo
subfiles.about: Reports a sharp rise in Japanese purchases of Sri Lankan graphite and scrap iron during 1931–1933.
subfiles.summary: Buell states that Japanese purchases during the first ten months of 1933 were more than three times their 1931 level and nearly twice their 1932 level. Two enclosures give destination-by-destination export figures for plumbago and for scrap iron and ores.

subfiles.title: Increased Purchases by Japan of Ceylon Plumbago
subfiles.from: Robert L. Buell, American Consul at Colombo
subfiles.about: Updates the Department on continued growth in Japanese imports of Sri Lankan graphite.
subfiles.summary: Buell calculates that Japan's monthly purchases rose from under 2,000 hundredweight in 1931 to about 7,000 during the latest four months. The enclosure compares monthly exports to Japan in late 1932–early 1933 with late 1933–early 1934.

subfiles.title: Exports of Ceylon Plumbago
subfiles.from: Brockholst Livingston, American Vice Consul at Colombo
subfiles.about: Reassesses earlier alarm over Japanese graphite imports by comparing Sri Lanka's exports across countries from 1930 through 1934.
subfiles.summary: Livingston finds that Japan's share had increased substantially but had declined from its early-1933 peak, while French and American shares were rising. He argues that changing trade conditions, prices, and competition provide a more plausible explanation than preparations for war. An enclosure tabulates first-quarter exports by destination for five years.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on LaVarre's Amazon report and missing Trinidad despatch
subfiles.from: William R. Manning, Division of Latin-American Affairs
subfiles.about: Discusses a missing Trinidad report alleging political motives behind Japanese settlement in the Amazon and how to answer William LaVarre.
subfiles.summary: Manning recalls a highly alarmist report claiming that Japanese agricultural colonies might eventually support an autonomous Japanese-controlled Amazon state, but considers the prediction almost entirely imaginary. He proposes a polite acknowledgment to LaVarre and asks Far Eastern Affairs to help locate the related Trinidad report.

subfiles.title: Letter reporting Japanese recalls and scrap purchases in South America
subfiles.from: William LaVarre
subfiles.about: Reports alleged recalls of young Japanese colonists from the Amazon and Japanese cash purchases of scrap metal in South American and West Indian ports.
subfiles.summary: LaVarre says Amazon and Marajó settlements were ordered to send men aged eighteen to thirty back to Japan. He also reports that the San Francisco Maru was loading old rails at Georgetown and questions whether Japanese colonists in the Amazon were genuinely agricultural laborers.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment of William LaVarre's letter
subfiles.from: Maxwell M. Hamilton, Assistant Chief, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.about: Acknowledges LaVarre's observations about Japanese activities in South America.
subfiles.summary: Hamilton states that the Department has noted the information with care. He thanks LaVarre for the spirit that prompted the report.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to memorandum on D. F. Giera's proposed explosives sale
subfiles.from: Department of State, Division of Western European Affairs
subfiles.about: References a memorandum alleging that D. F. Giera's explosives proposal concealed commissions on Japanese Military Mission purchases.
subfiles.summary: The sheet directs readers to another file for the underlying memorandum. It characterizes the proposed explosives sale as a possible commission scheme involving Giera and the Japanese Military Mission.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to memorandum on Du Pont machinery and explosives
subfiles.from: Department of State, Division of Western European Affairs
subfiles.about: References a discussion concerning Du Pont sales of machinery and explosives to the Japanese Government.
subfiles.summary: The sheet identifies Mr. Casey of Du Pont and Mr. Green as participants in the discussion. It notes that negotiations in the United States were being conducted by D. F. Giera for the Japanese Military Mission.

subfiles.title: Japanese loading of scrap steel at Curaçao and Aruba
subfiles.from: Russell M. Brooks, American Consul at Curaçao
subfiles.about: Reports a Japanese steamship's collection of scrap steel from oil companies in Curaçao and Aruba.
subfiles.summary: The vessel loaded about 1,200 tons of steel pipe at Curaçao and was expected to take another 2,500–3,000 tons at Aruba before visiting other West Indian ports. The purchases were arranged by West Indies Iron and Metal Exporters Limited of Montreal.

subfiles.title: Far Eastern Affairs note assessing a consular despatch
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.about: Briefly assesses the evidentiary value of an attached report on Japanese procurement.
subfiles.summary: The note indicates that existing conclusions rest largely on theories rather than firm evidence. It suggests that greater certainty will be possible unless the reporting officer obtains further information.

subfiles.title: Endeavors of Japanese Representatives to Obtain Raw Materials in the San Luis Potosí Consular District
subfiles.from: George P. Shaw, American Consul at San Luis Potosí
subfiles.about: Reports Japanese approaches concerning Mexican sulfur deposits and additional claims about sulfur and potash purchases.
subfiles.summary: Shaw confirms that Japanese representatives, working through Luis Iwadare, unsuccessfully sought control of sulfur deposits at Cerritos. J. H. Spranger supplied unverified information concerning Japanese interest in other Mexican sulfur holdings and a large potash contract in New Mexico allegedly intended for military use.

subfiles.title: Request for information on Japanese stockpiling
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.about: Raises the question whether Japan was accumulating strategic materials.
subfiles.summary: The brief note refers the stockpiling question to the military attaché in Tokyo. It serves as the departmental cover for the following military report.

subfiles.title: Imports of Commodities Essential to the Conduct of War
subfiles.from: T. Martin, Assistant Military Attaché; approved by William C. Crane, Military Attaché
subfiles.about: Analyzes Japanese imports of iron and nickel and evaluates whether they demonstrate wartime stockpiling.
subfiles.summary: The report compares six years of iron-ore, iron, scrap, nickel, exchange-rate, and military-budget figures. It concludes that most strategic imports did not show war-scale accumulation despite increased Army and Navy appropriations, although nickel appeared to be an exception and could support both coinage reserves and munitions manufacture.

subfiles.title: Interior Department inquiry about Alaska Railroad scrap exports
subfiles.from: T. A. Walters, Acting Secretary of the Interior
subfiles.about: Asks whether the State Department objects to a proposed Alaska Railroad sale of surplus scrap iron.
subfiles.summary: Walters forwards the general manager's letter and related correspondence concerning possible export to Japan. Pages 251 and 252 preserve duplicate versions of the inquiry.

subfiles.title: Alaska Railroad request for guidance on selling scrap to Japan
subfiles.from: O. F. Ohlson, General Manager, Alaska Railroad
subfiles.to: Harold L. Ickes, Secretary of the Interior
subfiles.about: Requests guidance on whether surplus Alaska Railroad scrap may be sold for export to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Ohlson encloses correspondence from Harry S. Kawabe and recalls a 1929 sale of 4,800 tons through a Portland broker for a Japanese purchaser. He says the earlier scrap was assumed to have reached the Japanese Government.

subfiles.title: Alaska Railroad reply to Harry S. Kawabe
subfiles.from: O. F. Ohlson, General Manager, Alaska Railroad
subfiles.about: Replies to Kawabe's request for prices on used rails and scrap iron.
subfiles.summary: Ohlson says the railroad does not presently have enough material to justify a sale. He offers to discuss the matter during his next visit to Seward.

subfiles.title: Request for a quotation on Alaska Railroad rails and scrap
subfiles.from: Harry S. Kawabe, Kawabe Investment & Trading Company of Alaska
subfiles.about: Requests a price for used steel rails and scrap iron delivered aboard ship at Seward.
subfiles.summary: Kawabe announces the opening of an importing and exporting business in Seward. He asks for a quotation per gross ton and proposes a future meeting with Ohlson.

subfiles.title: State Department response on Alaska scrap export
subfiles.from: William Phillips, Under Secretary of State
subfiles.about: States that the Department of State would not object to the proposed export of Alaska scrap iron to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Phillips acknowledges the Interior Department's October 11 inquiry and enclosure. He says that State would interpose no objection if the scrap were disposed of as proposed.

subfiles.title: Citizen protest against scrap-iron exports to Japan
subfiles.from: William J. Baer
subfiles.about: Argues that American scrap shipments to Japan could later be used against the United States in war.
subfiles.summary: Baer reports seeing or hearing of numerous scrap-laden vessels awaiting shipment to Japan. He calls the sales national suicide and also advocates independent American shipbuilding.

subfiles.title: Shipment of Scrap Metal to Japan
subfiles.from: Edward S. Benet, American Vice Consul at Cienfuegos; approved by Herman C. Vogenitz
subfiles.about: Details a 6,400-ton Cuban scrap-metal shipment to Japan and plans for another shipment.
subfiles.summary: Richard Nathan organized the transaction, with Sam Lewis purchasing from Cuban sugar mills and railroads; 1,800 tons were loaded at Havana and 4,600 at Cienfuegos. The Norwegian motor ship Tyr was to sail directly to Japan, and another similar shipment was anticipated in January 1935. Sources were the ship's agent O. K. Williams and Nathan's agent Sam Lewis.

subfiles.title: Purchases of Uruguayan Products for Presumed Military Uses
subfiles.doc_type: Confidential diplomatic despatch with duplicate copies
subfiles.from: Leon Dominian, United States Legation at Montevideo
subfiles.about: Considers whether prospective Japanese purchases of Uruguayan meat, wool, and hides might be connected with military preparations.
subfiles.summary: Dominian notes that Germany, Italy, and Japan—the countries most associated with accelerated armament—had attracted attention for purchases of Uruguayan commodities. He contrasts their interest with Spain's refusal to buy meat it did not need and suggests that the pattern may have military significance. The despatch appears three times: an original and two copies.

subfiles.title: Letter urging prevention of scrap-metal exports to Japan
subfiles.from: Lionel Friedmann
subfiles.about: Asks whether the government can prevent the heavy flow of American scrap metal to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Friedmann reports being told that Japan received 1,310,000 of the 1,400,000 tons exported during the year. He interprets the figure as evidence of preparation for war and requests preventive measures.

subfiles.title: Summary of Berlin despatch on Adrian Möller's trip to Japan
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.about: Summarizes a report that a German munitions-firm director was traveling to Japan, possibly to install arms-manufacturing machinery.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum identifies Adrian Möller as a director of a German machinery and munitions concern. It treats his journey as potentially connected with the installation of arms-production equipment.

subfiles.title: Visit of Representative of Eumuco Aktiengesellschaft für Maschinenbau to Japan
subfiles.from: P. C. White, Chargé d’Affaires ad interim, Berlin
subfiles.about: Reports that a director of a German machinery manufacturer was traveling to Japan under circumstances suggesting possible munitions work.
subfiles.summary: Initial information identified chief engineer Otto Simader, leading the Cologne consul to suspect machinery installation or ammunition manufacture rather than ordinary sales. A later report substituted director Adrian Möller, who planned to travel through New York en route to Japan.

subfiles.title: Report on Otto Simader's visa and proposed business trip to Japan
subfiles.from: Bartley F. Yost, American Consul at Cologne
subfiles.to: William E. Dodd, American Ambassador at Berlin
subfiles.about: Reports that Eumuco chief engineer Otto Simader obtained a transit visa for travel to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Yost regards it as significant that Simader was an engineer rather than a salesman. Because Eumuco manufactured machinery for producing munitions as well as presses and hammers, he suggests that the trip may concern equipment installation; competitors had reportedly sent representatives as well.

subfiles.title: White House referral of Lionel Friedmann's letter
subfiles.from: Louis McHenry Howe, Secretary to the President
subfiles.about: Forwards Friedmann's December 27 letter concerning scrap exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Howe refers the correspondent's letter to the State Department for handling. The paper records the White House's transfer of responsibility for the reply.

subfiles.title: Follow-up letter on scrap-metal exports to Japan
subfiles.from: Lionel Friedmann
subfiles.about: Renews Friedmann's unanswered request for measures against scrap-metal exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Friedmann repeats the figures given in his December 27 letter and stresses the importance of the subject. He asks the President for a response.

subfiles.title: Reply to Lionel Friedmann on legal authority over scrap exports
subfiles.from: Herbert Feis, Economic Adviser
subfiles.about: Explains that the federal government lacked legal power to restrict scrap-metal exports at that time.
subfiles.summary: Feis acknowledges both of Friedmann's letters and apologizes for the delayed response. He states plainly that the government could not then impose the requested restriction.

subfiles.title: Summary of Guaymas despatch on failed ship-scrapping venture
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.about: Summarizes the abandonment and apparent financial failure of a Guaymas ship-scrapping project intended to supply Japan.
subfiles.summary: The note attributes the project's collapse to labor problems and inadequate facilities. It also states that a recent scrap shipment from Guaymas was understood to have caused losses to the shippers.

subfiles.title: Shipment of Scrap Iron from Guaymas, Mexico, to Japan
subfiles.from: Guy W. Ray, American Vice Consul at Guaymas
subfiles.about: Reports a 6,000-ton scrap shipment to Japan and the failure of plans to dismantle additional vessels at Guaymas.
subfiles.summary: The Norwegian vessel Lionel departed with metal from three dismantled Mexican ships and large purchases from the Southern Pacific Railway of Mexico. Ray gives detailed prices and costs and concludes that promoters Ness and Dundisch lost heavily because of labor trouble, inadequate machinery, delays, and high expenses. Plans to bring in or dismantle more vessels were abandoned.

subfiles.title: Report on foreign purchasers of Cuban scrap metal
subfiles.from: Military intelligence source, author illegible
subfiles.to: Military Intelligence Division and Department of State
subfiles.about: Reports Cuban scrap-metal exports and continued purchasing by Japanese agents.
subfiles.summary: The poorly legible report states that about 10,900 tons of scrap were sent from Cuba to Japan and England during a specified 1933–1934 period. It adds that Japanese agents were continuing to buy all available scrap metal in Cuba and identifies a Havana commercial address.

subfiles.title: Scrap-metal shipments from Curaçao in 1935
subfiles.from: Russell M. Brooks, American Consul at Curaçao
subfiles.about: Describes Japanese-chartered collection of scrap from Curaçao, Venezuela, and Puerto Cabello.
subfiles.summary: The Japanese steamer Wazao carried scrap purchased by a Montreal exporter for Japanese importers, including about 1,500 metric tons from Curaçao and another 1,500–2,000 from the Maracaibo district. The vessel also called at Puerto Cabello, while refinery expansion and renewal were making unusually large quantities of metal available.

subfiles.title: Report on Japan's purchase of Polish zinc
subfiles.doc_type: Military intelligence report with distribution sheet
subfiles.from: Albert Gilmer, Colonel and Military Attaché
subfiles.to: Military Intelligence Division and distributed government offices
subfiles.about: Examines a Polish zinc sale to Mitsui and whether it concealed a broader military transaction.
subfiles.summary: The Giesche firm agreed to sell Mitsui about 5,500 tons of electrolytic zinc and 400 tons of zinc sheets, while Poland was to buy Japanese silk and cotton yarn. Investigation found no evidence that automobiles, guns, Germany, or a third country were secretly involved, and Gilmer characterized the deal as ordinary Japanese commercial expansion. A distribution sheet records circulation in April 1935.

subfiles.title: White House referral of Marcia Hamblet's telegram
subfiles.from: Louis McHenry Howe, Secretary to the President
subfiles.about: Refers Hamblet's warning about Japanese negotiations for a fuel-solidification process for immediate consideration and reply.
subfiles.summary: The White House asks State Department officials to consider and answer Hamblet's telegram promptly. A copy was also sent to the War Department.

subfiles.title: Telegram reporting Japanese interest in solidifying liquid hydrocarbons
subfiles.from: Marcia C. Hamblet
subfiles.about: Warns that Japanese representatives were seeking exclusive East Asian rights to a process for solidifying petroleum products and other liquids.
subfiles.summary: Hamblet describes a cheap, reversible process that would make fuels non-explosive, resistant to temperature extremes, and suitable for long-term wartime storage. She offers assistance because a contact was expected to leave New York on April 30 and supplies several business references.

subfiles.title: Memorandum coordinating investigation of Hamblet's allegations
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.about: Records arrangements with the Military Intelligence Division for responding to and investigating Hamblet's telegram.
subfiles.summary: Major Chipman had not yet received the White House copy sent to the War Department. State would acknowledge the telegram, while War, after consulting Navy, would decide whether to interview Hamblet.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment of Marcia Hamblet's telegram
subfiles.from: Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Acknowledges Hamblet's warning and states that it has been transmitted to the appropriate authorities.
subfiles.summary: The Department thanks Hamblet for making the information available. It informs her that the report has been brought to the attention of responsible agencies.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference on Japanese efforts to purchase scrap in Siam
subfiles.from: Baker, reporting from Siam
subfiles.about: References a report that a Japanese buyer arrived in Bangkok seeking up to 200,000 tons of iron and scrap.
subfiles.summary: The cross-reference points to despatch No. 200 in another file. It summarizes a Siamese newspaper report about large prospective purchases for a firm in Japan.

subfiles.title: Memorandum of conversation on the Hamblet investigation
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Green
subfiles.about: Records the War Department's conclusion that Hamblet's allegations about Japanese acquisition of a fuel-solidification process had no factual basis.
subfiles.summary: Colonel Burnett reviews the White House referral and the nature of Hamblet's April 25 telegram. He reports that the War Department investigated the matter, found the allegations baseless, and sent Hamblet a formal acknowledgment.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference on Chilean copper exports to Japan
subfiles.from: Scott, reporting from Chile
subfiles.about: References a report on approximately four million dollars in Chilean copper shipments to Japan over nine months.
subfiles.summary: The sheet directs readers to another file for despatch No. 404. Its summary records the approximate value and period of the copper exports.

subfiles.title: Note on scrap shipments from the Calgary district
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.about: Notes that large quantities of scrap iron for Japan were being shipped from the Calgary district.
subfiles.summary: The short note highlights Calgary as a source of substantial scrap shipments to Japan. It introduces the following Canadian consular report.

subfiles.title: Shipments of Scrap Steel to Japan Increase
subfiles.doc_type: Voluntary consular report quoting a newspaper
subfiles.from: Charles W. Allen, American Vice Consul at Calgary
subfiles.about: Reports a sharp increase in scrap-metal shipments from Calgary through Vancouver to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Allen reproduces a Calgary Herald article estimating that tens of thousands of tons were moving daily from the district. Foundry firms confirmed that shipments of relatively high-grade steel, iron, brass, and other metals had risen markedly during the preceding two weeks and were said to be destined for Japanese munitions manufacture.

subfiles.title: Italy salvages rails as scrap exports to Japan and Italy surge
subfiles.from: Metal Trade News Service
subfiles.about: Reports Italian recovery of disused streetcar rails and a major rise in American scrap exports to Japan and Italy.
subfiles.summary: Italian authorities ordered unused tracks removed and remelted to conserve war material. American Iron and Steel Institute figures showed Japan taking 65 percent of more than 3.75 million tons exported during the preceding thirty months, with Japanese annual purchases rising about 800 percent over the 1925–1932 average.

subfiles.title: Janson Steel & Iron Company letter protesting scrap exports
subfiles.from: Frank V. Kabel, Manager, Janson Steel & Iron Company
subfiles.about: Forwards a trade-press clipping and questions whether scrap exports should continue amid the prospect of war.
subfiles.summary: Kabel says the attached Daily Metal Market article speaks for itself. He warns that the United States may badly need the exported scrap in the near future.

subfiles.title: Routing note concerning Mr. Harding's proposed call
subfiles.from: Assistant Secretary's office
subfiles.about: Advises Hamilton that Mr. Harding of the Metals and Minerals Division would contact him about an attached matter.
subfiles.summary: The note identifies Harding by his Commerce Department division. Its context connects it with the inquiry about Japanese buyers of American scrap steel.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on identifying Japanese scrap-steel buyers
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.about: Records consultations with the Department of Commerce about Congressman Disney's request for the name of Japan's scrap-steel purchasing agent.
subfiles.summary: Harding initially said Japan had no known official agent and suggested referring Disney to the Japanese consul general, since Commerce ordinarily withheld company names. After reconsideration, he recommended a direct answer naming Mitsubishi Trading Company and Mitsui and Company as the leading commercial buyers in the United States.

subfiles.title: Congressman Disney's inquiry about Japan's scrap-steel agent
subfiles.from: Wesley E. Disney, Member of Congress
subfiles.about: Requests the name of the purchasing agent for Japanese scrap-steel acquisitions.
subfiles.summary: Disney asks for an immediate response identifying the buyer. The telegram prompted consultation between the State and Commerce Departments.

subfiles.title: Reply naming leading Japanese commercial scrap buyers
subfiles.from: William Phillips, Acting Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Identifies Mitsubishi Trading Company and Mitsui and Company as the leading commercial buyers of scrap for Japan in the United States.
subfiles.summary: Phillips replies that Mitsubishi's New York office and Mitsui's New York office were understood to be the principal buyers. The answer avoids characterizing either company as an official Japanese Government purchasing agent.
